messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mariam, a 63-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who worked as an auditor, came to treatment after years of trying to live around an event she had never fully been able to leave behind. Several years earlier, her adult daughter had been trapped during a violent incident while away from home, and Mariam had arrived too late to protect her. What stayed with Mariam was not only the knowledge of what had happened, but the brutal, helpless way she had learned of it: the disbelief in the voices around her, the awful realization that her daughter had been the one in danger, and the sense that the world could turn on someone she loved without warning. In the months afterward, Mariam found herself repeatedly returning to the details of that day, not by choice but because fragments would suddenly take over her mind and body. At times, a reminder of victims in the news or even a passing image of a frightened face would pull her back so completely that she felt the event as if it were happening again. She described these moments as if the memory arrived all at once, through every sense at once—what she saw, the sounds around her, the smell of the place, the feeling in her chest—and when it came, the terror was no less than it had been originally. She would freeze, convinced for a moment that she was back in that same helpless reality.

Certain places became difficult almost immediately. Mariam noticed that being in a locked or confined room made her skin prickle and her breathing shorten, especially if she could not quickly orient herself to the exits. She also began to dread natural settings that reminded her of where the original incident had occurred. If she was in a wooded park, near a trail, or anywhere that felt remote and exposed, her attention narrowed and she became overwhelmed by the sense that something terrible could happen there again. These reactions were especially hard because she had once enjoyed quiet outdoor spaces, but now a walk that should have been restful could leave her tense and searching the surroundings. She also avoided unfamiliar places more than she used to, telling herself that if she could not assess the danger in advance, she would be foolish to step into it. As an auditor, Mariam’s work sometimes required her to travel to different offices and sites, and she began choosing only locations she knew well. She arranged her day around predictability, declining some assignments and taking longer routes she had already memorized. In the office, she was careful about meeting rooms with closed doors and found herself more comfortable when she could sit near an exit, though she did not describe this to colleagues.

Over time, Mariam developed a constant state of watchfulness that she experienced as exhausting but necessary. She was superalert in public spaces, scanning people, entrances, and corners automatically, as though some part of her needed to catch danger before it reached her. At night, this vigilance did not switch off easily. She had trouble falling asleep and often woke in the middle of the night, her mind already racing ahead to possible threats. The body sensations that accompanied these moments made her feel betrayed by herself. She had come to believe that her body kept reacting as if she were still in danger even when she knew, logically, that she was safe at home or at her desk. That mismatch unsettled her deeply. She was also troubled by a growing belief that she could not stop bad things from happening, no matter how carefully she planned or how much she watched for warning signs. This sense of helplessness sat beside a broader loss of faith in people, life, and a higher power. Mariam said that she used to believe that goodness and order were stronger than violence, but after what had happened to her daughter, that belief had become difficult to hold onto.

By the time she sought help, Mariam’s life had narrowed around these experiences. She functioned, but only by staying on guard and keeping her world small. She was tired of feeling ambushed by her own memory and frightened by ordinary moments that could turn, without warning, into full reliving. What brought her in now was the sense that she could no longer keep living as if every unfamiliar place, every locked room, and every reminder of victims might open the door to that same unbearable terror. More than anything, she hoped for relief from the constant sense of threat and from the conviction that the world was no longer a safe or trustworthy place.
